definitions.text: The electric potential difference between two points in an electric circuit is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other.

Alessandro Volta (1745 –1827), an Italian physicist. One volt is the
potential difference between two points in a current carrying conductor
when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one
point to the other.

definitions.text: An instrument that measures potential difference and is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured.

periods.title: Introduction to Electric Current and Circuits
objectives: Define electric current and explain the flow of electrons in a conductor
Explain what constitutes an electric circuit
Identify the conditions required for current to flow in a circuit
periods.sequencing_rationale: These are the foundational concepts of electricity; students must understand what current is and how a circuit forms before exploring what drives current or resists it. This sets the stage for all subsequent topics.

periods.title: Potential Difference: The Driving Force of Current
objectives: Explain the concept of potential difference and its role in driving current
Relate potential difference to the movement of charges in a conducting wire
Describe how potential difference is measured and its units
periods.sequencing_rationale: Once students understand current and circuits, they need to grasp why current flows at all — introducing potential difference as the cause of current flow logically follows and sets up the concept of resistance.

periods.title: Resistance and Electrical Resistivity
objectives: Define resistance and explain its effect on current flow
Understand the concept of electrical resistivity as a material property
Differentiate between resistance and resistivity, and identify factors affecting each
periods.sequencing_rationale: With current and potential difference established, resistance is the next logical concept, explaining what opposes current flow. Resistivity extends this into material-based understanding, providing a bridge into circuit calculations.

periods.title: Series Combination of Resistors
objectives: Describe how resistors are connected in series
Explain why the same current flows through each resistor in series
Calculate equivalent resistance in a series combination through simple numerical examples
periods.sequencing_rationale: Once resistance is understood, students can explore how multiple resistors interact in a circuit. Series combination is introduced first as it is conceptually simpler and directly builds on the single-resistor case.

periods.title: Parallel Combination of Resistors
objectives: Describe how resistors are connected in parallel
Explain why potential difference remains the same across each resistor in parallel
Calculate equivalent resistance in a parallel combination through numerical examples
Compare series and parallel combinations in terms of current, voltage, and resistance behavior
periods.sequencing_rationale: Parallel combination follows series combination naturally, allowing direct comparison and reinforcing understanding of both configurations. This period requires more time due to the numerical practice involved in equivalent resistance calculations.

periods.title: Electric Power and Energy Consumption
objectives: Define electric power and its relationship to current, voltage, and resistance
Calculate electric power dissipated in circuits using relevant formulas
Relate electric power concepts to real-life energy consumption and appliance ratings
periods.sequencing_rationale: Electric power builds on all previously learned concepts (current, potential difference, resistance) and serves as a culminating, application-oriented topic that ties the unit together with practical relevance.

teaching_plan.planning_rationale: The content spans eight interrelated concepts building from foundational ideas (current, circuit) through causative and resistive properties (potential difference, resistance, resistivity) to circuit configurations (series and parallel combinations) and culminates in applied calculations (electric power). Given this is a beginner-level Grade 10 introduction, each conceptual block needs dedicated time to build understanding before moving to the next, with numerical practice periods (series/parallel combinations) requiring longer duration due to problem-solving components. Six periods allow logical grouping of closely related concepts (e.g., resistance with resistivity, current with circuits) while keeping each period focused and time-appropriate, without exceeding the maximum period limit or artificially inflating period count for closely related ideas.

Explain Ohm's law relationship: the potential difference across a conductor is proportional to the current through it, and therefore current is inversely proportional to resistance. Discuss factors affecting resistance: resistance is directly proportional to the length of a conductor, and resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area of a conductor. Introduce resistivity: electrical resistivity is a constant of proportionality that represents a characteristic property of a material showing how much the material resists electrical current flow, described further as a constant for a given metallic wire at a given temperature that represents the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges through it. Differentiate resistance (depends on dimensions) from resistivity (depends only on material). Introduce classification of materials: a component of a given size that offers a low resistance to the flow of electric current (good conductor), a conductor having some appreciable resistance, and a component of identical size that offers an even higher resistance than a poor conductor (insulator-like). Introduce rheostat: a component used to regulate current without changing the voltage source, and a device called rheostat is often used to change the resistance in the circuit.

Rheostat: regulates current without changing voltage

Equation (11.21) gives the rate at which electric energy is dissipated
or consumed in an electric circuit. This is also termed as electric power.
